claim: Mutations that increase fitness of bacteria at high antibiotic concentration often decrease fitness in the absence of antibiotic.
source: For example, mutations that increase fitness of bacteria at high antibiotic concentration often decrease fitness in the absence of antibiotic, exemplifying a tradeoff between adaptation to environmental extremes.
evidence: This is stated as a general observation about antibiotic resistance mutations in the abstract.

claim: The fitness landscape is nearly smooth at low and high antibiotic concentrations.
source: The landscape is nearly smooth at low and high concentrations, but the tradeoff induces a high ruggedness at intermediate antibiotic concentrations.
evidence: This is a primary finding stated in the abstract and supported by the model results.

claim: The tradeoff induces high ruggedness at intermediate antibiotic concentrations.
source: The landscape is nearly smooth at low and high concentrations, but the tradeoff induces a high ruggedness at intermediate antibiotic concentrations.
evidence: This is a primary finding stated in the abstract and demonstrated through modeling.

claim: All fitness maxima in the landscapes are evolutionarily accessible from the wild type.
source: Despite this high ruggedness, however, all the fitness maxima in the landscapes are evolutionarily accessible from the wild type.
evidence: This is a key finding proven mathematically in the paper.

claim: Selection for antibiotic resistance in multiple mutational steps is relatively facile despite the complexity of the underlying landscape.
source: This implies that selection for antibiotic resistance in multiple mutational steps is relatively facile despite the complexity of the underlying landscape.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the accessibility property.

claim: Sewall Wright introduced the concept of fitness landscapes in 1932.
source: Sewall Wright introduced the concept of fitness landscapes in 1932 (Wright, 1932), and for decades afterwards it persisted chiefly as a metaphor, due to lack of sufficient data.
evidence: This is a historical fact supported by citation.

claim: There are now a large number of experimental studies that have constructed fitness landscapes for combinatorial sets of mutations relevant to antibiotic resistance.
source: There are now a large number of experimental studies that have constructed fitness landscapes for combinatorial sets of mutations relevant to particular phenotypes, such as the resistance of microbial pathogens to antibiotics (Weinreich et al., 2006; DePristo et al., 2007; Marcusson et al., 2009; Lozovsky et al., 2009; Brown et al., 2010; Schenk et al., 2013; Goulart et al., 2013; Mira et al., 2015; Palmer et al., 2015; Knopp and Andersson, 2018), and the genomic scale of these investigations is rapidly growing (Wu et al., 2016; Bank et al., 2016; Domingo et al., 2018; Pokusaeva et al., 2019).
evidence: This is supported by multiple citations to empirical studies.

claim: Sign epistasis occurs when a mutation is beneficial in some genetic backgrounds but deleterious in others.
source: Conceptual breakthroughs, such as the notion of sign epistasis (where a mutation is beneficial in some genetic backgrounds but deleterious in others), have shed light on how ruggedness can constrain evolutionary trajectories (Weinreich et al., 2005; Poelwijk et al., 2007; Franke et al., 2011; Lobkovsky and Koonin, 2012; Zagorski et al., 2016).
evidence: This is a definition supported by citations.

claim: The fitness landscape of resistance genes depends strongly on antibiotic concentration.
source: In the context of antibiotic resistance, it has been realized that the fitness landscape of resistance genes depends quite strongly on antibiotic concentration (Mira et al., 2015; Stiffler et al., 2015; Ogbunugafor et al., 2016).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: Antibiotic concentration can vary widely in a patient's body and in various non-clinical settings.
source: This is highly relevant to the clinical problem of resistance evolution, since concentration of antibiotics can vary widely in a patient's body as well as in various non-clinical settings (Kolpin et al., 2004; Andersson and Hughes, 2014).
evidence: This is supported by citations.

claim: Antibiotic resistance often comes with a fitness cost such that a bacterium that can tolerate high drug concentrations grows slowly in drug-free conditions.
source: For example, it has been known for some time that antibiotic resistance often comes with a fitness cost, such that a bacterium that can tolerate high drug concentrations grows slowly in drug-free conditions (Andersson and Hughes, 2010; Melnyk et al., 2015).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: Tradeoffs between fitness and resistance are not universal.
source: While such tradeoffs are not universal (Hughes and Andersson, 2017; Durão et al., 2018), they certainly occur for a large number of mutations and a variety of drugs.
evidence: This is supported by citations.

claim: The dose-response curve of wild-type E. coli (strain K-12 MG1655) in the presence of ciprofloxacin can be fitted reasonably well by a Hill function.
source: Some of the present authors have recently shown that the dose-response curve of the wild-type E. coli (strain K-12 MG1655) in the presence of ciprofloxacin can be fitted reasonably well by a Hill function (Ojkic et al., 2019).
evidence: This is supported by citation to previous work by the authors.

claim: Similar scaling relations for dose-response curves have been reported previously by Wood et al., 2014 and Chevereau et al., 2015.
source: Similar scaling relations have been reported previously by Wood et al., 2014 and Chevereau et al., 2015.
evidence: This is supported by citations.

claim: In all cases where significant epistasis occurs in the E. coli data, it is negative.
source: Moreover, in all cases where significant epistasis occurs it is negative, that is the effect of the multiple mutants is weaker than expected from the single mutation effects.
evidence: This is based on analysis of data shown in Table 1.

claim: Every fitness peak is accessible from the wild type within the mutant selection window.
source: The preceding analyses have shown that within the mutant selection window, where mutants with higher fitness than the wild type exist, every fitness peak is accessible from the wild type.
evidence: This follows from the accessibility property.

claim: The reachability of the highest fitness peak is higher than the mean reachability of fitness peaks everywhere.
source: The reachability of the highest peak follows the qualitative behavior of the mean reachability, but remains higher than the mean reachability everywhere.
evidence: This is shown in Figure 7.

claim: The reachability of the fittest peak in the House-of-Cards model is around 0.018, an order of magnitude smaller than the lowest reachability in the tradeoff-induced landscape.
source: The reachability is found to be around 0.018, an order of magnitude smaller than the lowest reachability seen in the tradeoff-induced landscape.
evidence: This is based on numerical simulations comparing different models.

claim: The reachability of the fittest peak in the NK model is nearly 4 times smaller than the lowest reachability in tradeoff-induced landscapes.
source: Nonetheless, the reachability of the fittest peak (dotted pink line) is found to be nearly 4 times smaller than the lowest reachability in our landscape.
evidence: This is based on numerical simulations shown in Figure 7.

claim: In about 0.64 of the NK model landscapes, the fittest maximum is not reached in any of 32000 dynamical runs.
source: We found that in a fraction of about 0.64 of the landscapes, the fittest maximum is not reached in any of 32000 dynamical runs, indicating the absence of an accessible path in most of these cases (Schmiegelt and Krug, 2014; Hwang et al., 2018).
evidence: This is based on numerical simulations of the NK model.

claim: An evolutionary path always exists to any fitness peak in the tradeoff-induced landscapes.
source: In contrast, an evolutionary path always exists to any fitness peak in the tradeoff-induced landscapes, as we saw in the previous subsection.
evidence: This follows from the accessibility property proven earlier.

claim: All the allowed rank orderings in the model can be constructed without positive epistasis in fitness values.
source: In this context it should be noted that the rank orderings forbidden by the ordering condition all show positive epistasis for the fitness values, whereas all the allowed orderings can be constructed without positive epistasis.
evidence: This is a mathematical property of the model.

claim: The model's key results on accessibility only require the absence of positive epistasis.
source: As shown in Materials and methods, our key results on accessibility only require the absence of positive epistasis.
evidence: This is stated as a generalization of the model's assumptions.

claim: Ciprofloxacin inhibits DNA replication.
source: Marcusson et al., 2009 have constructed a series of E. coli strains with single, double and triple mutations conferring resistance to the fluoroquinolone antibiotic ciprofloxacin (CIP), which inhibits DNA replication (Drlica et al., 2009).
evidence: This is supported by citation.

claim: The dose-response curves of E. coli strains with ciprofloxacin resistance mutations were measured for the wild type, five single mutants, and eight double-mutant combinations.
source: Figure 2A shows the measured curves for the wild type, the five single mutants, and eight double-mutant combinations.
evidence: This is experimental data shown in Figure 2A.

claim: The intersection of dose-response curves of the wild type and a mutant defines the minimum selective concentration (MSC).
source: The intersection point is known as the minimum selective concentration (MSC), and it defines the lower boundary of the mutant selection window (MSW) within which the resistance mutant has a selective advantage relative to the wild type (Khan et al., 2017; Alexander and MacLean, 2018).
evidence: This is a definition supported by citations.

claim: Reciprocal sign epistasis is a necessary condition for the existence of multiple fitness peaks.
source: This fitness graph displays reciprocal sign epistasis, which is a necessary condition for the existence of multiple fitness peaks (Poelwijk et al., 2011).
evidence: This is supported by citation.

claim: The strains used in the experiments are isogenic derivatives of E. coli MG1655 with specific mutations in five different loci.
source: The strains are isogenic derivatives of MG1655, a K12 strain of the bacterium E. coli, with specific point mutations or gene deletions in five different loci: gyrA:S83L, gyrA:D87N, parC:S80I, ΔmarR, and ΔacrR.
evidence: This describes the experimental materials.

claim: The experiments measured optical density of bacterial cultures every 2-5 minutes to obtain growth curves.
source: We incubated bacteria in 96-well clear flat bottom micro-plates (Corning Costar) inside a plate reader (BMG LABTECH FLUOstar Optima with a stacker) starting from two different initial cell densities (half a plate for each), and measured the optical density (OD) of each culture every 2–5 min to obtain growth curves.
evidence: This describes the experimental methods.

claim: The time shift method was used to obtain exponential growth rates for each strain at different ciprofloxacin concentrations.
source: We then used the time shift method to obtain exponential growth rates for each strain and different concentrations of CIP, see Ojkic et al., 2019 for further details.
evidence: This describes the data analysis method with citation.

claim: Topoisomerase IV (gene parC) is a secondary target for ciprofloxacin with much weaker affinity than gyrase.
source: In particular, topoisomerase IV (gene parC) is a secondary target for ciprofloxacin with much weaker affinity than gyrase.
evidence: This is stated as biological knowledge.

claim: Mutations in parC do not contribute to ciprofloxacin resistance unless there is already a mutation in gyrA.
source: Therefore, mutations in parC do not contribute to resistance unless there is already a mutation in gyrA.
evidence: This is stated as biological knowledge.

claim: Combinations of mutations containing parC display positive epistasis.
source: As a consequence, in contrast to the mutants listed in Table 1, combinations containing parC display positive epistasis (Hughes and Andersson, 2017).
evidence: This is supported by citation.

claim: Fitness compensatory mutations do not exhibit adaptational tradeoffs.
source: In the case of antimicrobial resistance, there can be fitness compensatory mutations (Levin et al., 2000; Brown et al., 2010; Durão et al., 2018) that do not exhibit any adaptational tradeoffs.
evidence: This is supported by citations.

claim: Compensatory mutations generally emerge in a genetic background of mutations with adaptational tradeoffs.
source: These mutations are generally found in a population in the later stages of the evolution of antibiotic resistance, which implies that they emerge in a genetic background of mutations with adaptational tradeoffs.
evidence: This is stated as general knowledge about compensatory mutations.

claim: The property that dose-response curves intersect at most once holds for all functions used to represent dose-response curves in the literature.
source: This property holds for all functions that have been used to represent dose-response curves in the literature, such as the Hill function, the half-Gaussian or the exponential function, as well as for all concave function with negative second derivate (see Materials and methods for details).
evidence: This is proven in Materials and methods.
